entities.name: Pericles the Younger
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pericles the Younger, an Athenian strategos (general) executed in 405 BCE, was the illegitimate son of the renowned Athenian statesman Pericles and his brilliant Milesian consort, Aspasia. His brief but impactful military career unfolded during the final, tumultuous years of the Peloponnesian War, where he played a pivotal role in the Athenian navy's last major victory and, tragically, its subsequent catastrophic political fallout. His story highlights the brutal political realities and military desperation of late Classical Athens, particularly the severe penalties for perceived failure even among high-ranking commanders.

Appointed as one of the ten strategoi in 406 BCE, Pericles the Younger served alongside other prominent Athenians like Conon and Erasinides. His most notable engagement was the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE, a decisive naval victory for Athens against the Spartan fleet under Callicratidas, which temporarily broke the Spartan blockade of the Hellespont. Despite this crucial triumph, a severe storm prevented the Athenian commanders from rescuing shipwrecked sailors and recovering the bodies of the fallen. This failure led to a politically charged trial in Athens, where Pericles the Younger and five other generals were condemned to death under dubious legal pretexts.

The execution of Pericles the Younger and his co-commanders at Arginusae stands as a stark example of Athenian political instability and the harsh consequences of military defeat or perceived negligence, even in the face of victory. This event severely depleted Athens' experienced military leadership at a critical juncture, directly contributing to the city's final collapse in the Peloponnesian War just a year later at the Battle of Aegospotami. The trial and subsequent executions were later deemed illegal by the Athenians themselves, reflecting a period of profound self-reflection on their democratic processes and the dangers of mob rule.
